title: Millions burned on 26 spins

beats.narration: One wheel. One night. Millions gone.
Monte Carlo, August 1913. Black hit twenty-six times in a row. The room started chasing red. They said red was due.

The wheel has no memory. Ask the odds of black on spin twenty-seven. Divide the chance of twenty-seven blacks by the twenty-six that already fell. The powers cancel. Eighteen over thirty-seven remains. Same as spin one. Every bet against black chased a number that had already come true.
That fallacy still fires. Slot pulls. Coin flips. Your brain sees a pattern. The wheel does not.

mechanism: A fair single-zero roulette wheel has 37 pockets, 18 of them black, so each spin lands on black with probability 18/37 independently of every previous spin. By definition, the conditional probability of black on spin 27 given the first 26 spins is P(B1 ∩ … ∩ B27) divided by P(B1 ∩ … ∩ B26). Independence makes each of those a power of 18/37, and the ratio (18/37)^27 / (18/37)^26 collapses to 18/37 — the same odds as the very first spin. The 1-in-68-million number belongs to predicting the whole 26-spin streak in advance, not to the 27th spin after 26 blacks have already landed.

facts.claim: On 18 August 1913 the roulette ball at the Monte Carlo Casino fell on black 26 times in a row.
facts.quote: An example of the gambler's fallacy occurred in a game of roulette at the Monte Carlo Casino on August 18, 1913, when the ball fell in black 26 times in a row.

facts.claim: Gamblers that night lost millions of francs betting against black, believing the streak had to break.
facts.quote: Gamblers lost millions of francs betting against black, reasoning incorrectly that the streak was causing an imbalance in the randomness of the wheel, and that it had to be followed by a long streak of red.

facts.claim: On a single-zero roulette wheel the probability that a sequence of 26 spins comes out either all red or all black is about 1 in 68.4 million.
facts.quote: or around 1 in 68.4 million, assuming the mechanism is unbiased

facts.claim: The gambler's fallacy is the belief that an independent, equally probable outcome that has been under-represented becomes more likely on the next trial.
facts.quote: the belief that an independent and equally probable outcome which happened less frequently than expected is more likely to happen in the future (or vice versa)

facts.claim: For a fair chance mechanism, successive trials are statistically independent, so past outcomes do not shift the probability of the next one.

facts.claim: A European single-zero roulette wheel has 37 numbered pockets, 18 of them coloured black.
facts.quote: The pockets of the roulette wheel are numbered from 0 to 36.

facts.claim: On a European roulette wheel eighteen of the numbered pockets are black.
facts.quote: In number ranges from 1 to 10 and 19 to 28, odd numbers are red and even are black.
